Hypokinetic Diseases

  • Symptoms: Akinesia, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, stooped posture, reduced facial expression, small handwriting, and mood/cognitive issues.

Hyperkinetic Diseases

  • Degeneration of the indirect pathway in the striatum, causing involuntary movements similar to hemiballismus.

3. Dystonia:

  • Dysfunction in the direct pathway, resulting in sustained, twisting movements.

The Basal Ganglia:

  • The basal ganglia are a group of subcortical nuclei in the brain involved in regulating movement and coordinating motor activity. Key parts include:
    • Striatum: Consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen. It's the main input center for the basal ganglia, receiving information from the cerebral cortex. (Options C & D ruled out)
    • Globus Pallidus: Divided into the external (GPe) and internal (GPi) segments. It plays a role in the regulation of voluntary movement by processing signals from the striatum.
    • Substantia Nigra: Located in the midbrain and has two parts: the pars compacta (which produces dopamine) and the pars reticulata. It is involved in movement control and has a key role in the dopamine system. (Option B ruled out)
    • Subthalamic Nucleus: Located below the thalamus, it contributes to motor control by influencing the output of the globus pallidus. (Option A)

The basal ganglia use several key neurotransmitters to regulate motor control:

  1. Dopamine: Produced by the substantia nigra, particularly the pars compacta.
  2. GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid): The primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the basal ganglia. It is released by neurons in the striatum, globus pallidus (both external and internal segments), and substantia nigra (pars reticulata).
  3. Glutamate: The primary excitatory neurotransmitter. It is released by the cerebral cortex to the striatum and by the subthalamic nucleus to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra.

explanationHtml:
Option D: A second action potential will not occur.

  • After the initiation of a nerve impulse, there is a period during which a second stimulus will not cause a second action potential, no matter how strong the stimulus is. This refractory period during which a neuron is resting is known as the absolute refractory period.
  • The absolute refractory period occurs due to the inactivation of the voltage-gated sodium channels. It lasts for a short period (1-2 msec).
  • At point B, the action potential is in a depolarized state. A stimulus delivered at point B or C in the graph (the absolute refractory period) will not initiate a second nerve impulse.
  • Another refractory period occurs after the absolute refractory period. It is called the relative refractory period. During this period, the previously inactivated sodium channels open, but the voltage-gated potassium channels are still activated, leading to hyper-polarization.
  • As the membrane potential becomes more negative than the resting membrane potential, a stronger than usual stimulus is needed to initiate an action potential during this period.

Option A: A second action potential of normal magnitude will occur.

  • Action potential of normal magnitude will not occur because the stimulus is delivered during the absolute refractory period.

Option B: A second action potential of normal magnitude will occur but will be delayed.

  • A second action potential can only occur in the relative refractory period if the stimulus is strong enough. There will not be a second action potential in the absolute refractory period.

Option C: A second action potential will occur but will not have an overshoot

  • As the stimulus is given during the absolute refractory period, a second action potential will not occur and not have an overshoot.

Plasma proteins (such as albumin) are normally too large and negatively charged to pass through the glomerular filtration barrier. When the permeability of the glomerular capillaries increases (due to damage to the basement membrane or podocytes), the barrier becomes "leaky," allowing these large protein molecules to enter the renal tubule and appear in the urine (proteinuria).

  • The relevant concept is the selectivity of the glomerular filtration barrier.

    • Fenestrated endothelium

Cystometrogram Phases and Laplace's Law

Phases of Cystometrogram

  • Initial (Filling) Phase:
    • The bladder fills with sterile fluid.
    • Intra-vesical pressure (Pves) rises.
    • Detrusor muscle contracts, causing initial pressure increase without volume change.
    • Divided into three segments:
      • Phase I: Up to 1/3 of max capacity.
      • Phase II: 1/3 to 2/3 of max capacity.
      • Phase III: 2/3 to max capacity.
    • Provides insights into detrusor properties, especially in neurogenic bladders.
  • Emptying Phase:
    • Characterized by rhythmic external urethral sphincter contractions and increased Pves.
    • High-frequency pressure oscillations (HFPO) during active voiding.
  • Rebound Phase:
    • Post-voiding, Pves increases as a rebound effect.
    • Indicates residual pressure changes after voiding.

Application of Laplace's Law

  • Formula:
    P=2T/r
  • Where:
    • P = internal pressure
    • T = wall tension
    • r = radius
  • As the bladder fills, its radius increases, influencing pressure and tension.
  • Helps interpret pressure changes during filling and voiding, especially in detrusor overactivity or compliance issues.

Clinical Relevance

  • Key for diagnosing urological conditions:
    • Overactive bladder (OAB)
    • Bladder outlet obstruction
    • Neurogenic bladder dysfunction
  • Analyzing bladder pressure and compliance during each phase aids in personalized treatment strategies

  • Cheyne-Stoke respiration is a type of breathing disorder characterized by an abnormal breathing pattern consisting of cyclical episodes of hyperventilation and apnea.
  • Each cycle lasts between 30 seconds and 2 minutes.
  • Most commonly, it occurs during sleep but can also occur when the person is awake.
  • Cheyne stroke breathing is initiated due to changes that occur during periods of apnea.
  • The buildup of CO2 stimulates hyperventilation.
  • When a person breathes too much, i.e. expels too much CO2 from the lung blood and at the same time increases the O2 in the blood, several seconds pass before the changed lung blood can be transported to the brain and inhibits excessive ventilation.
  • At this point, the person has already over-ventilated for a few seconds.
  • When the over-ventilated blood finally reaches the brain's respiratory center, the center becomes excessively depressed, at which point the opposite cycle begins, CO2 increases and O2 in the alveoli decreases.
  • After a few seconds, the brain reacts to these new changes. When the brain responds, the person gasps again, and the cycle repeats.
  • Point W is the point of the respiratory center at which there is the maximum PCO2 in the brain. ( therefore triggering the deepest breaths)
  • Point Z: The point after respiration starts, as shown in the graph. Due to apnea, till this point, the PCO2 will become maximum in the lungs.

Incorrect Options:

Option A: XY

  • Point Y is the lowest PCO2 in the lung blood.
  • Point X is the end of respiration.

Option B: YZ

  • The PCO2 of lung blood gradually increases from point Y to point Z.

Option D: WX

  • Point W is the highest level of CO2 in the respiratory center.
  • Point X is the end of respiration.


Reference:

Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 13th Edition. Page No. 547

Single Breath Nitrogen Method

Principle

This method measures anatomic dead space using the single breath nitrogen washout technique

Procedure
  • The subject inhales a single deep breath of 100% oxygen.
  • Then exhales slowly and steadily.

Phases of Expired Nitrogen Curve
  • Phase I: Pure dead space air (no nitrogen).
  • Phase II: Mixture of dead space and alveolar air.
  • Phase III: Alveolar plateau (mostly alveolar gas).

Calculation

Explanation:

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognised discoveries related to regulatory T cells and immune tolerance, highlighting their central role in preventing autoimmunity.

FOXP3 is the master transcription factor required for the development and function of regulatory T (Treg) cells. Tregs are CD4+ lymphocytes that maintain immune homeostasis by suppressing excessive immune responses and preventing autoimmunity.

Mutations in FOXP3 cause IPEX syndrome (Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked), characterised by severe autoimmunity:

  • Autoimmune enteropathy

  • Type 1 diabetes mellitus

  • Eczema

  • Recurrent infections due to immune dysregulation.

Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (2025)

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to: Dr Mary E. Brunkow, Dr Fred Ramsdell and Dr Shimon Sakaguchi for:

  • Discovery of peripheral immune tolerance.

  • Identification and characterisation of Regulatory T cells (Tregs).

  • Expanding the understanding of immune regulation and prevention of autoimmunity.

Regulatory T Cells (Tregs)

Tregs are a specialised subset of CD4+ T lymphocytes responsible for maintaining peripheral immune tolerance and preventing excessive immune activation.

Origin

Tregs may develop as:

  • Natural Tregs (nTregs): Formed in the thymus.

  • Adaptive/Induced Tregs (iTregs): Derived from CD4+ T cells in peripheral tissues.

FOXP3 Gene

Development and function of Tregs are controlled by the Forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) gene.

Important points

  • Acts as the master regulator of Treg development.

  • Located on the X chromosome.

Functions of Tregs

Tregs suppress pathological immune responses and maintain self-tolerance by inhibiting the activity of various immune cells, including:

  • B lymphocytes

  • CD4+ T lymphocytes

  • Other effector immune cells

Mechanisms of Immune Suppression

  • Cytokine release

  • Granzyme- and perforin-mediated lysis of target cells

  • Interleukin-2 (IL-2)-linked apoptosis of effector T cells

These mechanisms prevent autoimmune disease and chronic inflammatory responses.

Clinical Significance

Mutations of the FOXP3 gene impair Treg function and result in IPEX syndrome, demonstrating the essential role of Tregs in immune regulation.

IPEX stands for:

  • I: Immunodysregulation

  • P: Polyendocrinopathy

  • E: Enteropathy

  • X: X-linked syndrome

Defective Treg function predisposes to severe autoimmune and chronic inflammatory disorders.

T helper 17 (Th17) cells (Option B): Th17 cells are pro-inflammatory CD4+ T cells involved in host defence against extracellular pathogens and autoimmune inflammation. FOXP3 does not regulate them.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ T cells) (Option C): CD8+ T cells mediate cell-mediated cytotoxicity against virus-infected and malignant cells. They are functionally distinct from Regulatory T cells and are not dependent on FOXP3 for their development.

Natural killer (NK) cells (Option D): NK cells are components of the innate immune system that destroy infected and malignant cells without prior sensitisation. They are unrelated to FOXP3-mediated immune tolerance
